identity.name: Kingdom of Navarre
alt_names: Kingdom of Pamplona (restored 1134, styled 'of Navarre' from Sancho VI)

land.text: the Navarrese part of the union of Aragon and Navarre; the cortes of Aragon and Navarre 'chose separate kings' in 1134

predecessors.note: Aragon's king had ruled Navarre since the partition of Pamplona in 1076 (kingdom-of-pamplona dossier).

land.text: the same kingdom restored: 'originally the Kingdom of Pamplona'

predecessors.note: Wikipedia treats Pamplona and Navarre as one kingdom (infobox 824-1841, Q200262); the Pamplona dossier of another group ends it in 1076, this one restarts it in 1134.

land.text: Iberian Navarre, 'Upper Navarre', annexed to Castile in 1515 after the invasion of 1512

successors.note: Lost 1512, reconquered May-June 1521, lost for good on 30 June 1521; 'permanently annexed in 1524' (Navarre page).

land.text: Lower Navarre, incorporated into France between 1620 and 1624

successors.note: Together with Béarn, under Louis XIII.

capitals.name: Pamplona (Iruña)
capitals.note: Infobox: Capital Pamplona (Basque Iruña). The page names no other royal seat before 1512.

capitals.name: Pau
capitals.note: Uncertain: after 1512 John III fled to Béarn (Orthez, Pau, Tarbes) and the Parliament of Navarre was later 'seated at Pau'; the pages opened name no capital of Lower Navarre (Saint-Palais hosted the Estates in August 1523).

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Cliopatria's first Navarre row starts in 1139, but the cortes of Aragon and Navarre 'chose separate kings' in 1134 and García Ramírez was elected. The page gives no inventory of his land (page silent), so Cliopatria's 1139 shape is carried back two years; it still holds La Rioja, which the page says was surrendered in 1136. The Zaragoza fief of 1135-1137 is a ledger event, not part of this shape.

correction.text: the kingdom of García Ramírez, 'the first King of Navarre to use such a title', elected 1134 by 'the nobility and clergy of Navarre'; La Rioja is inside until it is surrendered to Castile in 1136

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: '1136: García was obliged to surrender La Rioja to Castile' (the page). Cliopatria's 1139 shape has 16 cells in La Rioja; they are removed from 1136. Nothing else on the page changes the shape (the page is silent on Bureba, Álava and Tudela).

correction.text: Navarre without La Rioja, which García Ramírez was 'obliged to surrender to Castile' in 1136

keyframe_review.note: Cliopatria's 88-cell, 22,185 km2 shape for 1139-1201 includes La Rioja (16 cells), which the García Ramírez page gives to Castile in 1136; it also runs two years (1200-1201) past the conquest of the western provinces, which the Navarre page completes 'by 1200'. Corrected: the shape without La Rioja for 1139-1199; 1200-1201 is the new keyframe kingdom-of-navarre_1200. The Sancho VI page returns Artajona in 1157 (ledger) and the Navarre page puts Bureba and Rioja in Castilian hands by 1158. No infobox area exists for the 12th century (the infobox gives 10,000 km2 for 1300 only), so the area could not be compared.

correction.text: Navarre with Álava, Guipúzcoa and Biscay (western Navarre, conquered by Castile 1199-1200) but without La Rioja, surrendered in 1136; holds 1139-1199

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: 'By 1200 the conquest of western Navarre was complete. Álava became a county, Biscay a lordship, and Gipuzkoa a province' (the page). It equals Cliopatria's 1202 shape, which therefore starts two years late.

correction.text: Navarre after the loss of Álava, Guipúzcoa and Biscay to Castile; 'By 1200 the conquest of western Navarre was complete'

keyframe_review.note: 10,050 km2 for 1202-1284 against the infobox's 10,000 km2 for 1300 (ratio 1.0): the rump kingdom, about the modern Navarra plus a few cells of Lower Navarre. The Treaty of Guadalajara of 1207 confirmed the western conquests ('sealed a 5-year truce over the occupied territories' on the Navarre page), so no border moves 1202-1284 on the pages opened.

New keyframe: Cliopatria has no Navarre row for 1285-1332 (its Kingdom of France shape of 1300 contains 38 of the 41 cells of Navarre's 1284 shape). The page: 'The Kingdom of Navarre remained in personal union with the Kingdom of France until the death of King Charles I (Charles IV of France) in 1328', and 'King Charles was succeeded by his niece, Queen Joanna II'. Navarre stays a kingdom with its own cortes, so its shape is carried unchanged; the kingdom-of-france dossier draws the union as vassal_start 1284 / vassal_end 1328 (lighter tint). 1329-1332 was independent under Joanna II, so Cliopatria's gap to 1333 is also unexplained. Infobox 1300: 10,000 km2.

correction.text: Navarre in personal union with France 1284-1328, then under Queen Joanna II; the same land as 1202-1284

keyframe_review.note: 9,720 km2 (38 cells) against the infobox's 10,000 km2 for 1300 (ratio 0.97). None of the pages opened dates a border change 1333-1362; the Navarre page is silent on the treaties of Charles II's reign. Three cells in the Pyrenean north (about 43.3 N, 1.2-1.6 W, the Bidassoa and Cize side of Lower Navarre) are in the 1202-1284 shape, absent here, back in 1363-1374 and absent again from 1375: Cliopatria flicker that no page explains (gap, unverified: page budget).

10,098 km2: three more cells than the shapes before and after, for 1363-1374. Unverified: page budget. The Navarre page says Charles II (1349-87) 'gained and lost possessions in Normandy' but names no Iberian gain or loss, and is silent on the treaties of Pamplona, Aibar and Santa Cruz; the three cells (about 380 km2, the same Pyrenean cells near 43.3 N, 1.2-1.6 W as in 1202-1284) stay as Cliopatria has them, flagged as unexplained.
9,720 km2 for 1375-1421, the same 38 cells as 1333; Cliopatria drops the 1363-1374 cells again with no date on the pages opened (unverified: page budget).

Cliopatria's last Navarre shape (9,720 km2, 1422-1428). The kingdom continued, so the shape is extended unchanged to 1462, the year before Castile's annexation of the Sonsierra and Los Arcos was upheld at Bayonne; the page gives no border change between Charles III's death and 1463 (the 1451 civil war and 1479 succession move no land on the page).

correction.text: Navarre unchanged; the shape is carried from 1429 to 1462 although Cliopatria's row ends in 1428

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: 'The south-western tip, the Sonsierra (Oyon, Laguardia...) and Los Arcos, was occupied by Henry IV of Castile. Castile's annexation in 1463 was upheld by the French King Louis XI in Bayonne on 23 April 1463' (the page). A one-cell trim of the 1422 shape: the Los Arcos cell is inside it, Laguardia and Oyón are already outside.

minus.text: the south-western tip: the Sonsierra (Oyón, Laguardia...) and Los Arcos

correction.text: Navarre without the Sonsierra and Los Arcos, annexed by Castile and upheld at Bayonne on 23 April 1463

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: 'Lower Navarre (north of the Pyrenees) stayed independent under the House of Albret' after Ferdinand's conquest of Iberian Navarre in 1512; Upper Navarre was annexed to Castile in 1515. The 1529 Treaty of Cambrai 'sealed the division of Navarre along the Pyrenees'. Béarn was ruled by the same kings in personal union (the kingdom-of-france dossier uses Béarn as the 1589-1620 land) but is not Navarre territory and is not drawn here; Lower Navarre is a 30 km radius round Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port because the gazetteer has no Lower Navarre region. The ledger carries the 1521 reconquest and the 1525-1527 loss of Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port.

correction.text: Lower Navarre, the Ultrapuertos, the kingdom's land north of the Pyrenees

ledger.note: 1134: after Alfonso the Battler's death Navarre and Aragon 'chose separate kings' and García Ramírez, 'the Restorer', is the first to use the title King of Navarre. The Navarre page: 'the cortes of Aragon and Navarre chose separate kings'; the García Ramírez page: 'duly elected by the nobility and clergy of Navarre' (1134, no month; the Pact of Vadoluengo of January 1135 made Ramiro II of Aragon his 'father'). The page gives no boundary; Cliopatria's 1139 shape stands for the core.

region.text: the kingdom of Navarre restored under García Ramírez in 1134

ledger.note: 1135: García Ramírez holds Zaragoza as a fief. 'Before September 1135: Alfonso granted García Zaragoza as a fief' (García Ramírez page) after he declared himself Alfonso VII's vassal in May 1135. A short holding that no Cliopatria shape draws; surrendered in 1137.

region.text: Zaragoza, granted to García as a fief by Alfonso VII

ledger.note: 1136: García is forced to give up La Rioja. '1136: García was obliged to surrender La Rioja to Castile' (García Ramírez page); the Navarre page later calls the loss of Bureba and Rioja confirmed by the 1177 arbitration.

1137: Zaragoza is surrendered. 'García's Zaragoza holding was surrendered to Raymond Berengar in 1137, with Alfonso keeping suzerainty' (García Ramírez page). The recipient is the count of Barcelona as the page names him; the page does not say what office he held at Zaragoza.
1146: García occupies Tauste. '1146: García occupied Tauste, which belonged to Aragon' (García Ramírez page).
1146: Alfonso VII mediates peace between Navarre and Aragon over Tauste ('Alfonso VII mediated a peace between the two kingdoms'). The page does not say who kept Tauste; no shape change is drawn.
1157: Sancho VI recovers Artajona. 'Artajona was returned from Sancho III of Castile in 1157' (Sancho VI page); the page does not date its earlier loss. A town-sized change, below one cell.

region.text: Artajona, returned from Sancho III of Castile

ledger.note: 1173: Castilian invasions begin. 'Alfonso VIII's marriage to Eleanor gave Castile a pretext for invasions (1173-1176)' (Navarre page). The zone is Bureba and Rioja as the 1177 arbitration names them; the page does not name the ground of each invasion.

region.text: Rioja and Bureba, the lands in dispute with Castile

ledger.note: 1177: Henry II of England's arbitration settles the Castilian dispute. 'In 1177 Henry II of England's arbitration decided to refer them back to the boundaries' of 1158, 'which confirmed the loss of Bureba and Rioja' (Navarre page).

1199: Alfonso VIII invades western Navarre. 'Alfonso VIII launched a massive expedition against Navarre' while Sancho VII was abroad in Tlemcen; the Sancho VII page adds that Peter II of Aragon also invaded (the page dates Sancho's absence 'between 1198 and 1200').

1200: Castile completes the conquest of western Navarre. 'By 1200 the conquest of western Navarre was complete. Álava became a county, Biscay a lordship, and Gipuzkoa a province'; Treviño and Oñati were ruled directly from Castile. Navarre 'lost the provinces of Álava, Guipúzcoa, and Biscay to Castile' (Sancho VII page); the Treaty of Guadalajara of 1207 'sealed a 5-year truce over the occupied territories' and confirmed the conquests.

region.text: the provinces of Álava, Guipúzcoa and Biscay (western Navarre)

ledger.note: 1200: the fighting for western Navarre ends with the conquest complete; the 1207 truce at Guadalajara only confirms it.

region.text: the provinces of Álava, Guipúzcoa and Biscay (western Navarre)

ledger.note: 1234 (7 April): Sancho VII dies at Tudela and the crown passes to his nephew Theobald of Champagne. 'He died on 7 April 1234 in his castle at Tudela'; his nephew 'was recognized as his successor' (Sancho VII page; the Navarre page: 'passed by marriage to the House of Champagne' with the support of the cortes). Sancho's 1231 pact with James I of Aragon, that the survivor would inherit the other's kingdom, 'was never implemented'.

1284: Joan I of Navarre marries the future Philip IV of France and Navarre passes under the French crown. 'Philip IV married her in 1284'; 'From 1276... Navarre effectively passed into French control'; the personal union lasted until 1328 (Navarre page). The kingdom-of-france dossier draws it as a vassal tint 1284-1328.

1328: Charles I (Charles IV of France) dies and Joanna II succeeds, ending the union with France. 'King Charles was succeeded by his niece, Queen Joanna II'; regents were appointed on 13 March 1328 and ruled 'for 11 months' (to 27 February 1329) (Navarre page).

1463 (23 April): Castile's hold on the Sonsierra and Los Arcos is upheld at Bayonne. 'The south-western tip... was occupied by Henry IV of Castile. Castile's annexation in 1463 was upheld by the French King Louis XI in Bayonne on 23 April 1463' (Navarre page; the page does not date the occupation).

region.text: the south-western tip: the Sonsierra (Oyón, Laguardia...) and Los Arcos

ledger.note: 1479: John II dies and 'Queen Eleanor succeeded him for only 15 days and then died', leaving the crown to Francis Phoebus; Eleanor was Countess of Foix and Béarn, so the crown passes to the Foix line (Navarre page). In 1483 Catherine I succeeded her brother.

1512 (19 July): Ferdinand of Aragon invades Navarre. After the Fourth Treaty of Blois (18 July) 'the next day Ferdinand sent his troops across the border from Álava into Navarre' under the Duke of Alba (Spanish conquest of Iberian Navarre). The Navarre page: 'On 18 July 1512, Don Fadrique de Toledo was sent to invade Navarre'.

1512: Upper Navarre falls to the Spanish. 'the local authorities surrendered on 25 July' at Pamplona; 'By late August 1512, virtually all Iberian Navarre was under Spanish rule'; Tudela 'surrendered by 9 September'. The Cortes of Burgos on 11 June 1515 annexed it to Castile ('annexing the Basque kingdom to Castile in 1515'); the Navarre page says Parliament accepted Ferdinand as king on 13-24 March 1513 and annexation was 'as a separate kingdom with its own Courts'. Crown of Aragon forces (Alfonso of Aragon at Tudela) took part.

region.text: Iberian Navarre, later called Upper Navarre

ledger.note: 1512: the Albret court leaves Pamplona. After the invasion 'Jean d'Albret fled to Béarn (Orthez, Pau, Tarbes)' (Navarre page); the page names no capital of the exiled kingdom, so Pau, where the Parliament of Navarre was later seated, is a bridging guess.
1512: the Spanish hold Iberian Navarre; John III's October counter-attack on Pamplona fails (Navarre page: 'attacked Pamplona without success' in October 1512).

1521 (May): Pamplona revolts and the Franco-Navarrese reconquer Navarre. 'Pamplona revolted in late May 1521'; 'In less than three weeks, all of Navarre was reconquered' (Spanish conquest of Iberian Navarre).

region.text: all of Navarre, reconquered in less than three weeks

ledger.note: 1521 (30 June): the Franco-Navarrese are 'completely defeated at the Battle of Esquiroz' (Noáin) and Upper Navarre is lost again; the page says Southern Navarre was 'permanently annexed in 1524' on the Navarre page.
1521 (September): the second campaign opens at the Bidasoa. 'The second campaign began in late September 1521'; Hondarribia was captured on 12 October 1521.

region.text: Hondarribia (Fuenterrabía), taken by the Franco-Navarrese in October 1521

ledger.note: 1524 (19 February): Hondarribia surrenders. 'Pedro de Navarra's forces capitulated on 19 February 1524'; 'The Battle of Hondarribia would last until April 1524', and Charles issued a general pardon on 29 April 1524.
1525: Spain takes Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port. 'Spain captured it in 1525 and held it for almost two years.'

1527: local lords retake Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port ('Local lords retook it in 1527'); 'Spain abandoned the region in 1528, except for an outpost at Luzaide/Valcarlos'. The Treaty of Cambrai of 1529 'sealed the division of Navarre along the Pyrenees'.

1589: Henry III of Navarre becomes Henry IV of France. 'Henry III (reigned 1572-1610), succeeded to the throne of France as Henry IV in 1589' (Navarre page); Navarre stays a separate kingdom in personal union (kingdom-of-france dossier: vassal_start 1589).

1620: Lower Navarre passes to France. 'Between 1620 and 1624, Lower Navarre and Béarn were incorporated into France proper by Henry's son, Louis XIII' (Navarre page). 1620 is the start of the page's range and the year the infobox ends the last king (Louis II, 1610-1620); the kingdom-of-france dossier uses 1620.

region.text: Lower Navarre, incorporated into France proper

ledger.note: 1620: the Kingdom of Navarre ends as a separate kingdom, merged into France ('Between 1620 and 1624'); the Parliament of Navarre sits at Pau, and the French kings keep the title.

wars.name: García Ramírez's war with Alfonso VII
wars.outcome: '1137: García allied with Alfonso I of Portugal and confronted Alfonso VII'; '1139-1140: a peace between the two was confirmed'. The page names no treaty and no land changing hands.
wars.note: La Rioja had been surrendered in 1136, before the fighting; the page does not say what ground was fought over.

wars.name: Navarrese-Aragonese incident at Tauste
wars.outcome: García occupied Tauste, which belonged to Aragon; Alfonso VII mediated a peace between the two kingdoms.

wars.name: Castilian invasions of Navarre under Alfonso VIII
wars.outcome: Henry II of England's arbitration of 1177 'decided to refer them back to the boundaries' of 1158, 'which confirmed the loss of Bureba and Rioja'.
wars.note: Invasions dated 1173-1176 on the page; England is the arbitrator, not a belligerent.

wars.name: Castilian conquest of western Navarre

zones.text: the provinces of Álava, Guipúzcoa and Biscay (western Navarre)

wars.outcome: Álava, Guipúzcoa and Biscay lost to Castile by 1200; the Treaty of Guadalajara (1207) sealed a 5-year truce over the occupied territories and confirmed the conquests.
wars.note: The Sancho VII page has Peter II of Aragon invading with Alfonso VIII; it dates Sancho's absence in Africa 'between 1198 and 1200'.

wars.name: Navarrese civil war of the Agramonts and Beaumonts
belligerents: Beaumonts (supporters of Charles, Prince of Viana)
wars.outcome: 'In 1451 Navarre split in two confederacies, the Agramonts and the Beaumonts'; Prince Charles was 'defeated by his father at Aibar in 1451' and died in 1461. The page names no land changing hands.
wars.note: The end year is the death of Charles of Viana; the page does not give the end of the faction war.

wars.name: Spanish conquest of Iberian Navarre
wars.outcome: Castilian-Aragonese victory: Iberian Navarre annexed to Castile (Cortes of Burgos, June 1515); reconquests of 1516 and 1521-1524 failed; the Treaty of Cambrai (1529) 'sealed the division of Navarre along the Pyrenees', leaving Lower Navarre independent under the House of Albret.
wars.note: Infobox 1512-1529. Ferdinand declared war on France in March 1512; the Treaty of Noyon (14 August 1516) changed nothing; Pamplona 25 July 1512, Tudela 9 September 1512, Noáin/Esquiroz 30 June 1521, Hondarribia 19 February 1524.

certainty.note: Medieval frontiers are approximate. The only dated settlements are the 1177 arbitration (boundaries of 1158, Bureba and Rioja) and the 1463 sentence of Bayonne (Sonsierra and Los Arcos), both of which put a line on land the Navarre page names; the 1139 shape is Cliopatria's approximation.

Lower Navarre is a small kingdom whose Pyrenean edge with Spain was 'sealed' by the Treaty of Cambrai (1529); the Navarre page says the Treaty of the Pyrenees of 1659 'put an end to the litigation over the definite French-Spanish borders', so the line stays soft.

notes:
Dossier of the restored Kingdom of Navarre, 1134-1620. One kingdom or two (brief, section 6): Wikipedia has one article for Pamplona and Navarre (infobox 824-1841) and Cliopatria gives both rows Q200262. The eu-12-a dossier kingdom-of-pamplona ends the kingdom in 1076 (partition between Castile and Aragon) and says this dossier continues it from 1139; this dossier therefore restarts it in 1134 (the cortes of Aragon and Navarre choose separate kings) and lists kingdom-of-pamplona as predecessor. The reviewer may merge the two; if so cliopatria_names would carry both rows. Cliopatria's Navarre rows (1139-1428) are all reviewed here.
Cliopatria problems: (1) the 1139 shape includes La Rioja, surrendered to Castile in 1136; (2) its western provinces were conquered 1199-1200 but the shape runs to 1201; (3) no row for 1285-1332 (France's 1300 shape swallows Navarre) although Navarre stayed a kingdom in personal union; the kingdom-of-france dossier draws that as a vassal tint; (4) the row ends in 1428 although the kingdom lasted to 1620, so keyframes kingdom-of-navarre_1429 (as the extended _1422), _1463 and _1512 are new; Upper Navarre is the Castilian conquest of 1512-1515, Lower Navarre the Albret rump; (5) the 3-cell flicker in the Pyrenean north (absent 1333-1362 and from 1375, present 1202-1284 and 1363-1374) has no page and leaves the step from the 1284 shape to the 1333 shape unexplained.
Not settled: the rulers strip is omitted (page budget; no list page opened); the Navarre page is silent on the treaties of Charles II's reign (Pamplona, Aibar, Santa Cruz de Campezo) and the Évreux dynasty; García Ramírez's vassalage to Alfonso VII from May 1135 and Navarre's recovery of La Rioja in Alfonso VIII's minority are not on the pages opened (Castile's dossier should carry vassal_start kingdom-of-navarre 1135 if the Castile group's pages give it); the Sancho VI page is silent on the Castilian wars; the date of Navarre's loss of Artajona; Sancho VII's 'vassal territories 1196-1203' are unnamed on his page. Page conflicts: Amaiur 3 October 1521 or 19 July 1522 (conquest page itself inconsistent); Hondarribia taken 12 October 1521 (other sources 6 October).
Counterparts: crown-of-castile covers 1512-1529 although Cliopatria's row ends in 1515 (Spain's Crown of Castile continues); crown-of-aragon, county-of-barcelona, kingdom-of-castile, kingdom-of-aragon, kingdom-of-france are other groups'. Béarn is ruled in personal union with Navarre 1512-1620 but is not drawn as Navarre territory. Names the gazetteer lacks (real places and a historical region): Artajona, Tauste, Laguardia, Los Arcos, Oyón, Hondarribia, Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port, Pau, La Bureba. Page budget (5): Kingdom of Navarre, García Ramírez, Sancho VI, Sancho VII, Spanish conquest of Iberian Navarre; the Navarre page was read twice with different prompts.
